Property was seized, teachers' fathers were beheaded, and bishops fled.
There were four persecutions: the Antonine, the Severan, the Decian from 249 to 251, and the Diocletianic from 303 to 311.
The last two did most to shape formation.
Origen himself was jailed and tortured under Decius.
In those years the church's whole authority was persuasion.
Our writings describe souls and books far more than rooms and walls, so we cannot tell you where believers gathered.
Eusebius gives us the remembered account of Origen's boyhood house:
About the year 202, under the emperor Severus, persecution struck Alexandria.
Leonides was arrested and held for beheading.
His son Origen was sixteen.
Eusebius tells what happened next in that house.
He wrote a century later, from our church's memory, from Origen's own letters and from reports about him.
The boy burned to give himself up and die beside his father.
His mother begged him to spare her, but he would not listen.
So she hid all his clothes, and shame kept him at home.
Origen did the one thing left to him.
He wrote to his father in prison.
One line of that letter survives, "Take heed not to change your mind on our account."
Leonides did not change his mind.
He was beheaded, and the family's property was seized.
Not yet seventeen, Origen was left the eldest of seven children, and his mother was a widow.

text:
What our record holds is danger that came and went over three centuries before 325. Property was seized, teachers' fathers were beheaded, and bishops fled. There were four persecutions: the Antonine, the Severan, the Decian from 249 to 251, and the Diocletianic from 303 to 311. The last two did most to shape formation. Origen himself was jailed and tortured under Decius. In those years the church's whole authority was persuasion. Our writings describe souls and books far more than rooms and walls, so we cannot tell you where believers gathered. Eusebius gives us the remembered account of Origen's boyhood house:

About the year 202, under the emperor Severus, persecution struck Alexandria. Leonides was arrested and held for beheading. His son Origen was sixteen. Eusebius tells what happened next in that house. He wrote a century later, from our church's memory, from Origen's own letters and from reports about him.

The boy burned to give himself up and die beside his father. His mother begged him to spare her, but he would not listen. So she hid all his clothes, and shame kept him at home.

Origen did the one thing left to him. He wrote to his father in prison. One line of that letter survives, "Take heed not to change your mind on our account."

Leonides did not change his mind. He was beheaded, and the family's property was seized. Not yet seventeen, Origen was left the eldest of seven children, and his mother was a widow..
